Spain has become an active laggard in European and international climate policy, and that the process of EU enlargement and Europeanization has not necessarily promoted policy convergence, but may have contributed to the development of a ‘Spanish way’ in environmental policy-making.

Spain has been developing an active role in European and international climate change negotiations, that this role is not necessarily promoting the convergence of Spanish and European policies and that the European Union is not necessarily the most important factor explaining Spanish policies on climate change.
Spain is no laggard in European and international climate negotiations, and that Europeanization has not necessarily led to policy convergence between Spain and the European Union.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether Spain is developing an active role in the European and international climate policy process and, if so, how it is doing so.
explaining the role of Spain as a ‘laggard’ within the European Union, and with the implications of this role for the European integration process.
the role that the European Union plays in shaping the national climate policy of a member state.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the case of Spain and climate change, Europeanization is not a straightforward process of policy transfer, and that the European Union is not a unitary actor in international negotiations.
, in spite of its efforts, Spain remains an active but still reluctant laggard in the European and global fight against climate change.
Spain’s role in climate policy is that of an active laggard.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Spanish government has been more active in defending its national interests in the EU, and has been able to do so with some success, while at the same time the process of European integration has been more effective in shaping national policies than in producing a convergence of policies between member states.
the European Union is a ‘greening’ force, but not an equalizer of environmental policies.

Spain’s role in the European climate policy arena is more complex than is often assumed.
the EU’s climate policy is not a ‘one-size-fits-all’ model that is easily transposed from one member state to another.
